props.title: Ed Wood
props.initialSlug: Oddball biopic of Hollywood's worst director ever

sections.content: Tim Burton's Ed Wood stands as the definitive love letter to Hollywood's most infamous "worst director." Johnny Depp captures Wood's boundless optimism and cross-dressing peculiarities while making movies like Plan 9 from Outer Space (1959) and Glen or Glenda (1953). The film's masterstroke is Martin Landau's Oscar-winning turn as Bela Lugosi, showing the faded horror icon's friendship with Wood during his final years. Shot in gorgeous black-and-white, Burton recreates the DIY spirit of 1950s B-movies, celebrating passionate outsider filmmaking rather than mocking it.

sections.content: The film fits into a rich tradition of movies about moviemaking, but with a crucial twist - instead of celebrating genius, it champions determined mediocrity. Like The Disaster Artist (2017) about Tommy Wiseau's The Room (2003), it finds nobility in the pure passion to create, regardless of talent. Burton's film shares DNA with Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962) in its portrait of Hollywood's dark edges and forgotten stars. SUBHEAD: The Real Hollywood Underbelly

Ed Wood reveals the scrappy side of 1950s Hollywood, where dreamers scraped together micro-budgets and shot in days. This reality contrasts sharply with glossy studio productions like Singin' in the Rain (1952). The film's treatment of Lugosi's morphine addiction and career decline mirrors later stories of Hollywood casualties like Auto Focus (2002) about Bob Crane's seedy demise. Burton uses Wood's story to explore the thin line between delusion and determination that drives many filmmakers.
